title: Oracle Materialized View Refresh: Fast, Complete, On Commit
description: Refresh an Oracle materialized view with DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH: complete vs fast refresh, materialized view logs, ON COMMIT, schedules and EXPLAIN_MVIEW.

reviewNotes: Written from the Oracle 19c docs; no example has been run, all output blocks are expected output and need a test run on 19c/23ai. Please verify: (1) STALENESS shows STALE (not UNKNOWN) for the first on-demand view after the insert; (2) the EXPLAIN_MVIEW output rows and message texts for the SUM-without-COUNT query (modelled on doc Example 5-9; exact rows may differ, especially REFRESH_FAST_AFTER_INSERT, which may be N if the log check fails); (3) MLOG$_ORDERS is the generated log table name; (4) the claim that a non-atomic complete refresh can leave the view visibly empty (docs say it uses TRUNCATE); (5) the 19c doc text lists lowercase 'f' for fast in DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH, uppercase 'F' is widely used, confirm it works; (6) MAT_VIEW REWRITE ACCESS plan operation name. The DBMS_SCHEDULER example needs CREATE JOB privilege.

data.text: To refresh a materialized view in Oracle, call DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH with the view name and a method: 'C' for a complete refresh, 'F' for a fast (incremental) refresh, or '?' to let Oracle choose. You can also make Oracle refresh it for you, either at every commit (ON COMMIT) or on a schedule (START WITH ... NEXT ...).

Which option is right depends on how fresh the data must be, how big the view is, and whether your query qualifies for fast refresh. This tutorial builds one small summary view and walks through every refresh option on it, with the dictionary queries you need to check what actually happened.
How materialized view refresh works

A normal view stores only a query. A materialized view stores the result of the query as a real table. Reads are fast because the work is already done, but the stored rows go out of date as soon as someone changes the base tables (Oracle calls them master or detail tables). A refresh brings the stored rows back in line with the base tables.
Every materialized view has two refresh settings. The method decides how the rows are rebuilt. The mode decides when the refresh runs.

content: Truncates or deletes the stored rows and runs the full defining query again
Applies only the changes recorded since the last refresh
Fast refresh if possible, otherwise complete. This is the default
Only when you call a DBMS_MVIEW refresh procedure. This is the default
As part of every commit that changed a base table
After every DML statement on a base table (fast refresh only, strict join rules)
Automatically at the times you give

data.text: So if you write CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... AS SELECT ... with no refresh clause at all, you get REFRESH FORCE ON DEMAND: nothing refreshes until you ask, and when you ask, Oracle tries fast first. Many people expect a materialized view to update itself and are surprised when it never changes.
Sample setup
Run this in a test schema. It creates an orders table with five rows across three customers.

data.caption: Sample orders table

data.text: Your user needs the CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW system privilege (or a role that has it) to follow along.
Complete refresh on demand
Start with the simplest case: a summary of order count and total amount per customer, refreshed only when you ask, and always rebuilt in full.
Step 1: create the materialized view

data.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW customer_sales_mv
  BUILD IMMEDIATE
  REFRESH COMPLETE ON DEMAND
AS
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*)    AS order_count,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amount
  FROM orders
 GROUP BY customer_id;

SELECT * FROM customer_sales_mv ORDER BY customer_id;
data.caption: Complete refresh, on demand

data.text: BUILD IMMEDIATE (the default) runs the query now and fills the view. With BUILD DEFERRED the view stays empty until the first refresh, which must be a complete one.
Step 2: change the base table and see the stale data

data.caption: New order, then check the view

data.code:
CUSTOMER_ID ORDER_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
----------- ----------- ------------
        103           1           75

MVIEW_NAME          STALENESS  LAST_REFRESH_TYPE LAST_REFRESH
------------------- ---------- ----------------- ----------------
CUSTOMER_SALES_MV   STALE      COMPLETE          2026-11-15 09:10
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The view still says customer 103 has one order. That is expected: an on-demand view does not move until you refresh it. The STALENESS column in USER_MVIEWS tells you the stored rows no longer match the base table. Other values you may see are FRESH, UNUSABLE (built deferred, never refreshed), UNKNOWN and NEEDS_COMPILE.
Step 3: run the refresh

data.caption: Complete refresh with DBMS_MVIEW

data.code:
CUSTOMER_ID ORDER_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
----------- ----------- ------------
        103           2          375
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: In SQL*Plus or SQL Developer you can write the same call as EXEC DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH('CUSTOMER_SALES_MV', 'C');. A complete refresh re-reads the whole orders table every time. That is fine for five rows. For a view built over hundreds of millions of rows it can take a long time, which is why fast refresh exists.
Fast refresh with a materialized view log

A fast refresh applies only the rows that changed. To know what changed, Oracle needs a materialized view log on each base table. The log is a separate table that records every insert, update and delete on the base table until the dependent views have consumed it.
Step 1: create the log

data.caption: Log on the orders table

data.code:
MASTER   LOG_TABLE
-------- -------------
ORDERS   MLOG$_ORDERS
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Each part of the log definition has a job. For a view with aggregates, the Data Warehousing Guide requires all of these:

items.content: WITH ROWID: record the rowid of each changed row.
The column list (customer_id, amount): every column of the table that the view uses.
INCLUDING NEW VALUES: store new values as well as old ones, so Oracle can subtract the old amount and add the new one.
SEQUENCE: ordering information, needed when the table gets a mix of inserts, updates and deletes.

data.text: Step 2: create a fast-refreshable view

data.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW customer_sales_mv
  BUILD IMMEDIATE
  REFRESH FAST ON DEMAND
AS
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*)      AS order_count,
       SUM(amount)   AS total_amount,
       COUNT(amount) AS amount_count
  FROM orders
 GROUP BY customer_id;
data.caption: Fast refresh, on demand

data.text: Notice the extra COUNT(amount) column. For a fast-refreshable aggregate view, COUNT(*) must be in the select list, and each aggregate such as SUM(amount) or AVG(amount) needs its matching COUNT(amount). Oracle uses these counts to know when a group becomes empty after deletes. Leave them out and fast refresh after updates or deletes is not possible.

If you add a log to a table that already has a materialized view, do one complete refresh of that view before the first fast refresh. Otherwise the fast refresh fails with ORA-12034: materialized view log younger than last refresh.
Step 3: change data and fast refresh

data.caption: Update, delete, then fast refresh
Check the result

data.code:
CUSTOMER_ID ORDER_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
----------- ----------- ------------
        101           1          250
        102           2          575
        103           2          375

LAST_REFRESH_TYPE STALENESS
----------------- ----------
FAST              FRESH
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Customer 101 lost an order, customer 102's total rose by 50, and LAST_REFRESH_TYPE confirms Oracle used the fast path. The pending-changes count shows a few rows in the log before the refresh (the exact number depends on how Oracle records the update). After the refresh those rows are purged, because by default the log is purged right after refresh once no other view still needs them.
Automatic refresh: ON COMMIT and scheduled refresh
ON COMMIT: always current

data.caption: Switch to ON COMMIT

data.code:
ORDER_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
----------- ------------
          2          310
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: No refresh call was needed. The view changed as part of the commit. The price is that every commit on orders now does extra work, so commits get slower. On a busy OLTP table that cost is paid by every user who writes to it.

If the refresh fails at commit time, Oracle writes the list of views it could not refresh to the alert log, and you have to refresh them by hand. ON COMMIT is also not supported for views over remote tables, and once it is set you cannot run distributed transactions against the master table.
Scheduled refresh: every 30 minutes

data.code:
ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW customer_sales_mv
  REFRESH FAST ON DEMAND
  START WITH SYSDATE
  NEXT SYSDATE + 30/1440;
data.caption: Refresh every 30 minutes

data.text: START WITH is the first run. NEXT is a date expression evaluated after each refresh to get the next run time; 30/1440 is 30 minutes as a fraction of a day. For daily at 2 AM you would write NEXT TRUNC(SYSDATE) + 1 + 2/24. You cannot combine START WITH or NEXT with ON COMMIT, which is why the statement switches back to ON DEMAND first.

Many DBAs prefer to leave the view ON DEMAND and create a DBMS_SCHEDULER job that calls DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH. You get run history and error messages in USER_SCHEDULER_JOB_RUN_DETAILS, and you can chain the refresh after the batch load that feeds it.

data.code:
BEGIN
  DBMS_SCHEDULER.CREATE_JOB(
    job_name        => 'REFRESH_CUSTOMER_SALES',
    job_type        => 'PLSQL_BLOCK',
    job_action      => 'BEGIN DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH(''CUSTOMER_SALES_MV'', ''F''); END;',
    repeat_interval => 'FREQ=MINUTELY; INTERVAL=30',
    enabled         => TRUE);
END;
/
data.caption: Same schedule with DBMS_SCHEDULER

data.text: Why fast refresh fails, and how to find out
When a view cannot be fast refreshed, Oracle tells you with one of these errors:

content: ORA-23413: table does not have a materialized view log
Fast refresh requested but a base table has no log
ORA-12015: cannot create a fast refresh materialized view from a complex query
The query uses something fast refresh cannot handle
ORA-12052: cannot fast refresh materialized view
Rowids missing from a join view, or the inner table of an outer join has no unique constraint on the join columns
ORA-12034: materialized view log younger than last refresh
Log created after the last refresh of the view

data.text: Instead of guessing, ask Oracle with DBMS_MVIEW.EXPLAIN_MVIEW. It writes its findings to MV_CAPABILITIES_TABLE, which you create once by running the utlxmv.sql script from $ORACLE_HOME/rdbms/admin. You can pass an existing view name or just a query you are planning to use.

data.code:
@?/rdbms/admin/utlxmv.sql

BEGIN
  DBMS_MVIEW.EXPLAIN_MVIEW(
    'SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
       FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id');
END;
/

SELECT capability_name, possible, SUBSTR(msgtxt, 1, 50) AS msgtxt
  FROM mv_capabilities_table
 WHERE capability_name LIKE 'REFRESH%'
 ORDER BY seq;
data.caption: Explain why a query is not fast refreshable

data.code:
CAPABILITY_NAME                 P MSGTXT
------------------------------- - ----------------------------------------
REFRESH_COMPLETE                Y
REFRESH_FAST                    N
REFRESH_FAST_AFTER_INSERT       Y
REFRESH_FAST_AFTER_ONETAB_DML   N SUM(expr) without COUNT(expr)
REFRESH_FAST_AFTER_ONETAB_DML   N COUNT(*) is not present in the select list
REFRESH_FAST_AFTER_ANY_DML      N see the reason why REFRESH_FAST_AFTER_ONETA
REFRESH_FAST_PCT                N PCT is not possible on any of the detail ta
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Read it from the top. REFRESH_FAST_AFTER_INSERT means insert-only changes could be applied fast. REFRESH_FAST_AFTER_ONETAB_DML is N, and the message names the fix: add COUNT(*) and COUNT(amount). Fix the reasons one by one and run it again until the capabilities you need show Y. Delete old rows from MV_CAPABILITIES_TABLE between runs so you do not mix results.

Some features rule out fast refresh entirely. The documented list includes non-repeatable expressions such as SYSDATE and ROWNUM, analytic functions such as RANK, CONNECT BY, the MODEL clause, subqueries in the select list, and RAW or LONG RAW columns. For join views, the rowid of every table in the FROM list must appear in the select list.
atomic_refresh: what readers see during a refresh
DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH has an atomic_refresh parameter that matters a lot for complete refreshes.

content: Deletes and re-inserts rows in one transaction
Readers keep seeing the old data until commit. Slower, more undo and redo
Truncates the view, then reloads it, and can use parallel DML
Faster, but readers can see an empty or partly loaded view while it runs

data.code:
BEGIN
  DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH(
    list           => 'CUSTOMER_SALES_MV',
    method         => 'C',
    atomic_refresh => FALSE);
END;
/
data.caption: Non-atomic complete refresh

data.text: Use atomic_refresh => FALSE for large views refreshed in a batch window when nobody is reading them. During business hours keep the default. Oracle 12c and later also offer out_of_place => TRUE, which builds the new data in a separate table and swaps it in, so the view stays readable while the refresh runs.

When you pass several views in one call with atomic_refresh left as TRUE, they are refreshed in a single transaction. If one fails, none of them are updated. That is good for consistency, but one broken view can hold back all the others.
Common mistakes

items.content: Expecting a view with no refresh clause to update itself. The default is ON DEMAND. Check REFRESH_MODE in USER_MVIEWS.

Using FORCE and assuming fast refresh happens. FORCE silently falls back to complete. Check LAST_REFRESH_TYPE after a refresh; if it says COMPLETE on a view you designed for fast refresh, run EXPLAIN_MVIEW.
Missing COUNT columns. An aggregate view without COUNT(*) and COUNT(expr) can only fast refresh after inserts, if at all.

A log nobody consumes. If a view that used a log is dropped or stops refreshing, the log keeps growing. Logs are purged only after every dependent view has refreshed. Check the size of MLOG$ tables from time to time.
ON COMMIT on a busy OLTP table. Every writer pays the refresh cost at commit. Measure commit times before and after in a test system.

Assuming ALTER to FAST was validated. Oracle checks fast refresh eligibility when you create the view with REFRESH FAST, but not when you change it to FAST with ALTER. The error only appears at the next refresh.

data.text: Performance tips

items.content: Gather statistics on a materialized view after you create it, just like a table. The CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW documentation says this explicitly.
Index the columns people filter on. Indexes are maintained during refresh, so keep them to the ones you need.
Batch many small changes into one transaction when the view is ON COMMIT. The refresh then runs once at commit instead of per change.
Refresh views that depend on the same tables together, or use DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH_DEPENDENT with the table name to refresh all views built on it.

If you want the optimizer to use the view automatically for queries against orders, add ENABLE QUERY REWRITE. It is off by default. You can confirm a rewrite in the execution plan, where the view shows up as MAT_VIEW REWRITE ACCESS.

data.text: For reading those plans, see how to read an explain plan in Oracle.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between fast refresh and complete refresh in Oracle?

A complete refresh runs the full defining query again and replaces all rows. A fast refresh reads the materialized view log and applies only the changes since the last refresh. Fast refresh needs logs on all base tables and a query that meets the fast refresh rules.
How do I check when a materialized view was last refreshed?
Query USER_MVIEWS (or DBA_MVIEWS): LAST_REFRESH_DATE gives the time, LAST_REFRESH_TYPE says FAST or COMPLETE, and STALENESS says whether the data still matches the base tables.
How do I refresh a materialized view every 30 minutes in Oracle?

Use ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_name REFRESH START WITH SYSDATE NEXT SYSDATE + 30/1440, or create a DBMS_SCHEDULER job with repeat_interval => 'FREQ=MINUTELY; INTERVAL=30' that calls DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH.
Can I query a materialized view while it is being refreshed?

Yes. With the default atomic refresh, readers see the old rows until the refresh commits. With atomic_refresh set to FALSE, a complete refresh truncates the view first, so readers can see it empty for a while.
Does a materialized view refresh automatically when the table changes?
Only if you created it with ON COMMIT (or ON STATEMENT). Otherwise it changes only when you call DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH or when its START WITH / NEXT schedule fires.
Summary

items.content: Default refresh is FORCE ON DEMAND: nothing happens until you call DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH.
Use method 'C' for complete, 'F' for fast, '?' for force.
Fast refresh needs a materialized view log WITH ROWID, SEQUENCE, the used columns and INCLUDING NEW VALUES.
Aggregate views need COUNT(*) and COUNT(expr) for every SUM or AVG to fast refresh after updates and deletes.
Run DBMS_MVIEW.EXPLAIN_MVIEW to see exactly why fast refresh is not possible.
Check STALENESS, LAST_REFRESH_TYPE and LAST_REFRESH_DATE in USER_MVIEWS after every change you make.
Use ON COMMIT only where the extra commit time is acceptable; otherwise schedule the refresh.
Keep atomic_refresh TRUE while users are reading; use FALSE in batch windows for big complete refreshes.

linkedin.post:
Your Oracle materialized view shows yesterday's numbers even though the table changed. Here is why.

A materialized view with no refresh clause is FORCE ON DEMAND. It never updates by itself.

→ Refresh by hand: DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH('MY_MV', 'C') for complete, 'F' for fast, '?' to let Oracle choose.
→ Fast refresh needs a materialized view log on every base table: WITH ROWID, SEQUENCE, the used columns, INCLUDING NEW VALUES.
→ Aggregate views need COUNT(*) plus COUNT(amount) next to SUM(amount), or fast refresh after updates and deletes is not possible.
→ Not sure why fast refresh fails? Run DBMS_MVIEW.EXPLAIN_MVIEW. It tells you the exact missing piece.
→ Check USER_MVIEWS: STALENESS, LAST_REFRESH_TYPE and LAST_REFRESH_DATE show what really happened. FORCE can quietly fall back to complete.

ON COMMIT keeps the view current but makes every commit on the base table slower. Scheduled refresh (NEXT SYSDATE + 30/1440) is often the safer choice.

Which do you use in production: ON COMMIT, scheduled refresh, or a manual refresh after the batch load?
